newsitem.title: UK: Spector wins British court fight for song rights.
newsitem.headline: Spector wins British court fight for song rights.

text.p: Legendary U.S. record producer Phil Spector on Friday won a British court battle over the rights to his first hit and the prospect of thousands of pounds (dollars) in back royalties.

Justice Francis Ferris ruled in the High Court in London that Spector, 57, owned the rights in Britain to the music and lyrics of "To Know Him is to Love Him", which The Teddy Bears took to the top of the U.S. charts in 1958.
Spector had argued that a 28-year copyright assignment to Warman Music in 1958, which then granted a licence to British-based Bourne Music Ltd, had expired in 1986.

Bourne rejected this, but has now lost its rights in respect of the song in Britain. The song title was inspired by the epitaph on the tombstone of Spector's father who committed suicide when Spector was eight.
The case began in January, when the reclusive Spector put in a rare public appearance, arriving at the High Court in central London in a limousine. He was not in court for the verdict.
He has spent much of the past 20 years at his mansion in California and has produced nothing of note since working with U.S. punk group The Ramones in 1980.

Spector's name will forever be associated with a string of classic three-minute pop singles in the 1950s and early 1960s featuring his 'Wall of Sound' production that "filled out" recordings in a way no one had previously achieved.
One of his best-known records, "River Deep, Mountain High" by Ike and Tina Turner, flopped in the United States when it was first released in 1966, prompting a first retreat from the music industry.
He worked on the Beatles' "Let It Be" album, although Paul McCartney hated his string accompaniment on "The Long and Winding Road", citing this as one of the reasons why he decided to go solo.
